concepts.name: Matrix as a Transformation
concepts.summary: A matrix is a linear transformation: it moves every vector consistently, bending space in one fixed way. A 2×2 matrix carries the unit circle onto an ellipse; the semi-axis lengths of that ellipse are the matrix's singular values, and their directions are its principal axes.

concepts.name: Singular Value Decomposition
concepts.summary: Every matrix M factors as M = U·Σ·Vᵀ: a rotation Vᵀ (orthonormal input directions), a diagonal stretch Σ of singular values σ₁≥σ₂≥…≥0, then a rotation U (orthonormal output directions). Rotate, stretch, rotate. It always exists and the singular values are unique; all stretching lives in Σ. (Upstairs: the same factorization underlies low-rank adaptation of trained weight matrices.)

concepts.name: Singular Values
concepts.summary: The diagonal entries of Σ, sorted σ₁≥σ₂≥…≥0, measuring how far a matrix stretches space along each principal direction — the energy each direction carries. For many real matrices, and especially for differences of two nearby matrices, they decay fast: a few large, then a long tail near zero, with an elbow. (Upstairs: fast decay is why weight updates are effectively low-rank.)

concepts.name: Low-Rank Approximation
concepts.summary: Keep the top r singular values (zero the rest): M ≈ U_rΣ_rV_rᵀ, with U_r (d×r), Σ_r (r×r), V_rᵀ (r×d). Eckart–Young: this truncation is the provably closest rank-r matrix to M, minimizing ‖M−M_r‖. When σ decay fast a small r captures almost everything, compressing d² numbers to 2dr. (Upstairs: this is the mathematics behind LoRA / low-rank adaptation.)
